speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Car-leton):
speechtext:
On many occasions this session questions appearing on the order paper have been asked to stand as orders for returns. I would like to ask the government whether the answers to these questions, when brought down, appear anywhere on the records of the House, or are they simply handed to the member asking for the return?

Questions Passed as Orders
They appear in the Votes and Proceedings.
A great many of these questions are matters of public interest, and the replies should be available to hon. members.

In cases where questions stand as orders for returns, when the information is made available a few days or sometimes a few weeks later, it is tabled, and any hon. member who is interested in the return can get a copy of it from the proper officials.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I wish to corroborate the view apparently held by the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell). What I understood him to press was this: when questions are made to stand as orders for returns there is no record of the returns in Hansard or in the Votes and Proceedings, and the result of having it so stand is to prevent that publicity being given to the answers which is desirable in many cases. I know it is the right of the government under the rules to have a question stand as an order for return; it is a right that has been very generally exercised-I think too loosely exercised this session. It should be confined only to cases where the record is very long and there is no great importance as to publicity; it should not be done simply as a means of ridding the order paper of the question.
It was not done under the late government, I suppose?
Very rarely.

The remarks of the right hon. gentleman are correct in every respect except one, and that is that every return tabled in the House is immediately registered in the Votes and Proceedings and can be there found. Then those returns are submitted to the Printing Committee, and the Printing Committee decides which returns shall be printed and which shall not be printed.
It is quite true that a note is made in the Votes and Proceedings when a return is tabled, but the return itself does not appear in the Votes and Proceedings.
But you get it from the clerk in charge of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think we might have a useful thought in the matter in this way. Many of the questions that are asked this session are too long, too elaborate, and call for information which I do not think is of
practical value. The right of a member to ask a question we do not dispute, but I would suggest to hon. members who put questions on the order paper that they ought to observe the rule with regard to brevity in a larger measure than they do.

If I am not out of order, perhaps I may be permitted to intrude on delicate ground and say that in the case of some questions that have been asked of one of my departments, I have discovered that the member in whose name they stood had not put them on the order paper and had no information concerning them. I think members should not allow outsiders particularly, to put questions on the order paper until after full consultation with them, and until they know what those questions really mean. In the case of some of these questions, one or two of them at least, it would take quite a staff working at least a month to prepare the answer. That is easier, of course, for some outside person, than paying a legal man to get the information and work up the case.
As to questions being changed to orders for returns, questions may look innocent, but when they are taken to the departments it is found that they mean pages and pages of information, and I 'submit that Hansard never was intended to be the medium through which all the records of departments are published. It was intended to be the medium through which the expressions of the members should be recorded, and to give certain other information at moderate length, but not infomation that would cover pages of Hansard.

I do not at all take exception to the general principle the minister lays down, namely, that questions on the order paper should not be used as a means of getting private information merely for
citizens._They should only he used as a
means of getting information in the general public interest, and, further some regard should be had to the time and expense entailed in procuring that information. I never was so impressed in my life with the need of that as three years ago, when one hon. member moved that the government procure from Great Britain a list of all the shareholders and debenture holders in the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which return no doubt cost this country many thousands of dollars, which return came over in a large box, and which box I am informed never was opened.
They are still in a box.

May I inquire if any
steps will be taken to have this condition

Questions Passed as Orders
remedied; that is where questions appearing on the order paper are passed as orders for returns, will the answers be incorporated in the Votes and Proceedings or in Hansard?-I do not care which so long as we get the information.

I may inform the hon.
gentleman that no paper is tabled in the House without reference being made to it in the Votes and Proceedings of the next day. For instance, any reports or any returns that were tabled yesterday are mentioned in today's Votes and Proceedings. As to the inclusion of these bulky returns in Hansard, I think it would certainly entail too large an expense and that it is really uncalled for. As the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) said quite clearly a moment ago, the remedy is in the hands of any member who has an interest in any particular return. He can go before the Printing Committee and there move for the printing of the return. I have done it quite often myself when I was on the floor of the House, and it is done, very often in relation to important matters. Surely hon, members null not ask that Hansard be overloaded with bulky returns.

Somebody will have to assume the authority for deciding which returns are to appear in Hansard and which are not. This must not be left to the Hansard staff because it would not be fair to place upon them the responsibility. Either the Speaker of the House, or the Clerk, or Clerk Assistant, or the government, will have to decide which of these returns are to appear in Hansard. These returns sometimes appear as answers to questions. Very often a minister with a lengthy answer will say, "I will not read this but will hand it to Hansard," and then Hansard prints it.

A return was laid on the Table yesterday in reference to some question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Carleton relating to a matter of general interest to the people of this country and a matter which has been discussed in the House this session. I tried to get a look at the return brought down, but I was informed that the hon. member for Carleton had it and consequently I have not been able to see it.

Every member is entitled to get a copy of a return. If he will only apply to the proper clerk here in the department, as many copies can be had as are desired. We have a staff of nearly eighty typists and stenographers who are there for that purpose.

The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) stated a moment ago that three years ago an order of the House was passed for a list of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk and that it cost the country a lot of money to get this list, that the names were contained in a box, and that that box was never opened. I may say to the leader of the Opposition that he is badly informed. The box was opened, and we found out that the government had not complied with the order of the House, that the list of shareholders contained in the box was not the list as of the date asked for. It was a useless list. So the leader of the Opposition is wrong again.

The box was not opened for some time after it was returned here. I made inquiries and found out. I called the matter then to the attention of the hon. member who moved for the return. Perhaps he has opened the box since, and it is quite evident that the object he had in seeking the information was not shown to be served by the contents when he opened the box.

The box was
opened ten days after it came in.
Another case of misinformation.

Supply-Public Works

It must be a pretty small mining company to be shipping that quantity of coal a year. I would like to invite the attention of the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie), who represents a Cape Breton constituency, to the fact. If the hon. member appeals to me for information about the matter-
I know it will be accurate.

Yes, it will be accurate. I know the place very well and the necessity exists for this work. It is not in my own riding, it is in the fair county of Inverness which is part of Cape Breton Island. My hon. friend will easily find out, as far as coal is concerned, that the northern coast of the county of Inverness from Port Hood to Cheti-camp, about fifty miles, is one solid mass of coal, as yet undeveloped, and we have no railway there-for which I am sure my hon. friend will be sorry-except for a distance of thirty-five miles from Canso down to the town of Inverness. The rest of the coast, covering about twenty-five miles, has no railway at all. The mine in question, although not large, is shipping considerable coal to Prince Edward Island, the distance from Chimney Corner to that market being comparatively short-some thirty miles. The development that is now going on at Chimney Comer is small because there is no harbour. This breakwater is to serve the purpose of a harbour. When the breakwater is extended there will be shelter for vessels coming, in there, and I can assure my hon. friend that, for the protection of the fishermen and the people generally who have to do business at that place, fishing and mining, the extension of this breakwater is most important.

Halifax Dredging Company.

How deep is it proposed to dredge there?-$1.45 is a very high price.

My hon. friend should have regard to the nature of the material. This is not considered a high price in the department, because this is largely rock that is being removed from the channel, and

it is expensive work. Twenty-two feet is the depth, to conform with the other portion of
the channel.
That is 22 feet at low water?
Yes.
Is that rock in boulders, or in ledges?
Boulders, largely.

When was the work
authorised?
It was let in August of last year by order in council after tenders had been called for and received.
There was no vote for this last year?
We were doing the work under our general vote and we could probably have proceeded in that way, but it was thought better to vote a separate sum this year for the work.

In 1922-23, a total of 16,981 yards was removed, at an expenditure of $24,622.

It is proposed to remove 56,500 yards this year, at a cost of $81,925.

Does the minister know who compose the Halifax Dredging Company?

tenders.

Last session I inquired of the minister if any representations had been made on behalf of the people of Grand Manan and the neighbouring islands urging upon the government the necessity for the construction of breakwaters in all or any of these islands. I was informed by him later that representations had been made, and he gave me the names of the places where works were to be constructed. I am disappointed now to find nothing in the estimates in connection with what I consider were representations made by the patronage committee of my county. As I stated last session, prior to the general election assurances were given the 60
people of the islands that if the present administration were returned to power breakwaters and other necessary structures would be built to help the fishing industry in which the people there are engaged. Does the government intend to adopt any of the representations made? If so, what work will be undertaken this year?

There are many
works we would like to undertake in the county of Charlotte, but unfortunately the money available is not sufficient. It may be somewhat disappointing to my hon. friend that more items do not appear in the estimates for his county, but we can only carry on such work as in the judgment of the department is urgent. Supplementary estimates will be brought down later, but in their preparation I am not sure what consideration is being given to further expenditures in the county of Charlotte.

Can the minister assure
me that something will be included in the supplementary estimates to carry on a portion of the work covered by the representations to which I referred?

I am very sorry
I cannot meet my hon. friend's proposal. The matter will be considered carefully by the government when the supplementary estimates are being made up.

What representations have been made to the government with respect to the island of Grand Manan? Its population are wholly dependent upon the fishing industry, and I submit that they are entitled to quite- as much consideration as the people in the county of Inverness, where thousands and thousands of dollars are being spent in every little cove; also the county of Cape Breton North and Victoria seems to have swallowed up a very large portion of the vote for Nova Scotia. Here is a population producing, I am satisfied, more fish, than the whole island of Cape Breton, but not a dollar appears in the estimates for their protection.

The files of the
department would disclose the representations that have been made. Those files are available to my hon. friend if he cares to look into them.

What is the meaning of
the term, "patronage committee"?

I have not anything here on the patronage committee and am not able to answer my hon. friend's question.

have been made regarding this work, and we are obtaining a report upon it.
What amount was spent last year?
Why is it necessary to have an appropriation of $40,000 when the expenditure of that amount is not contemplated?

The expenditures last year were in the nature of repairs at Back bay, Bathurst, Bayside, Black river, Burton, Campbelton, etc.-quite a number of small expenditures. Several items are noted for expenditure this year, but only some six or eight as yet.

I noticed that the premier of New Brunswick was here the other day and I was very credibly informed that one of his missions was to unload on the Dominion the provincial government wharves , in tidal

waters, especially those on the St. John river. I may say that not a cent has been spent on the repair of these wharves since before the war. They are in an extremely dilapidated condition, and if the government takes them over they will be a liability rather than an asset. I will point out further that in many cases there are duplications of provincial and Dominion wharves, especially on the St. John river, and that is something the minister ought to look into before he agrees to have this legacy unloaded upon him. I understand that negotiations are under way between the two governments, and I would like to know what their present status is and what are their prospects.
I understand from my hon. friend that he is opposed to the Dominion government becoming involved in the provincial wharves in New Brunswick.
I did not say that.

The matter has been before the government for some time. A survey of these wharves was made in 1918 or 1919 and the late government apparently did have it in mind at one time to take them over. There was a similar proposal from British Columbia, and that province was more successful; we did get a transfer of the provincial wharves to the federal government. The government has given the matter consideration but has not yet definitely made up its mind whether or not these wharves shall be taken over. The matter will be under further consideration in the course of the next few days.
The minister must not misconstrue any remarks I made. I did not either affirm or deny the proposition. I have a very definite opinion upon the subject myself.
What is it?

I think the minister should take over those wharves that are not duplicates of other wharves, but where there is duplication I do not think the federal government should take them all over and maintain two where only one is necessary I think that is a sound position to take, and one that public opinion will support. The premier of New Brunswick went back to the province the other day and said that all he was waiting for was an order in council to put this matter through. Is that correct?

An order in council would bring the wharves under the supervision of the Dominion government, but

Supply-Public Works
money would have to be voted for repairs and renewals. I assure my hon. friend that a very careful survey of the situation will be made before action is taken; in fact, I think it has already been made by the department.
Has that order in council been passed, or is it contemplated?
An order in council has not been passed.

At the time when the Hon. Mr. Carvell was Minister of Public Works, this matter was gone into exhaustively. A list of the wharves was prepared, their values were ascertained by the department, and an order in council was drafted. This will all be on the departmental files. The people of New Brunswick-it does not matter what administration was in power there-were led to believe that the wharves would be taken over by the federal government. There may be criticism on the ground that the provincial government has not in the meantime made any expenditure on the wharves, but the fact is that as a result of the abstinence in that respect of both the federal and provincial authorities, the wharves are, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) says, in a pitiable condition. It seems to me that the matter of these wharves is a federal matter just as much as a railway would be, and I would like to see it dealt with on a business basis. It ought to be possible for the two governments to get together. I do not want to suggest anything in the House that will help any sort of political claptrap down in New Brunswick, such as the premier stating that he is only waiting for an order in council. I want to get away from all that political bombast and give consideration to the interests of the people who need the facilities of these wharves, which constitute an important part of the highway of commerce. I would like to see something definite done, and done quickly. I do not think the minister will be subjected to any criticism from those sitting on this side representing New Brunswick if he does act, and we will not find any fault if there should be a little bit of generosity in the action.

Last year $60,000 was
voted for Nova Scotia under the head of harbours and rivers generally, repairs and improvements, and the amount is the same this year. The figures for other provinces are as follows: Prince Edward Island, $14,000 last year and the same amount this year; New Brunswick, $65,000 last year, $40,000 this year; Quebec, $75,000
each year; Ontario, $65,000 each year; Manitoba $15,000 each year; British Columbia $95,000 last year and $75,000 this year. If it is reasonable to take $25,000 from New Brunswick and $20,000 from British Columbia this year, why would it not be possible to make a similar reduction in the votes for the other provinces, especially in view of the minister's intimation that in each case a less amount was required during the year than had actually been voted? I am not seeking to deprive any province of what is its just due or requirement, but there appears to be discrimination against New Brunswick and British Columbia in this respect. If a similar reduction is made in the other cases, very substantial saving will result. I would also point out that, deducting the revote, we have new work this year to the extent of $1,289,000, covering all the provinces-a very considerable sum indeed. So I suggest that the minister might make a saving in the other provinces similar to that in the two I have mentioned.

The vote for New Brunswick last year was larger than was considered necessary for a contingency vote. There was a question at that time of taking over these wharves in New Brunswick. That not having been done, in making up bur estimates this year we deducted the sum of $25,000 from last year's vote. In regard to British Columbia, the deduction is arrived at in this way. The Dominion government took over the wharves in 1918, I think, and since that time we have been putting the former provincial wharves in a state of good repair. That having been done, it was found that this year we could get along with a smaller vote for British Columbia.

The minister told us that only $11,000 had been spent out of this vote for New Brunswick. I think that is altogether too small for the province, because I myself know of wharves owned by this government which are quite out of repair and need attention. What is the modus operand! in arranging for these repairs? Does the engineer make regular trips of inspection? I know the engineer on the St. John river very well, and he is a very good man. Does he make inspection trips, and of his own motion make recommendations, or does he wait until somebody draws the attention of the government to some particular wharf, and then act under instruction?

The district engineer is charged with the responsibility of taking care of these works, and it is upon his recommendation that the expenditure is made.
Supply-Public Works

If my hon. friend has in mind any works that ate in a bad state of repair, he might very well bring them to the attention of the department, and we will have inquiry made.

I have in mind the wharves at Gagetown and at Oromocto. I ask the question to find out if the minister would take reccommendations from me, for instance, if I called his attention to the matter, or does the engineer himself go round and see what is required?
He is supposed to make his inspection trips from time to time.

As the minister has reduced this vote by $25,000 this year, that seems to me to indicate that he is very doubtful about taking over these tidal wharves. The amount was larger last year when this subject was under consideration, but now there is a reduction of $25,000. We have heard with interest that British Columbia has had her tidal wharves transferred: I think it was in the year 1919. I hope the minister will keep this matter in view, but it does not look to me as if the transfer of these wharves was seriously contemplated when we see this reduction of $25,000. I hope I am mistaken in that view.

Perhaps the minister would reply to the question of my colleague. I hope the government has not determined not to take these wharves over, but if that is the fact, and if this reduction in the estimate points to that, let us have the blow, however bad it may be. I trust, however, that the government has not come to that conclusion, because there are at least two subjects in the province of New Brunswick that I trust some day will be effectively dealt with. One is the taking over of these wharves, and the other I shall not discuss at present; I refer to the taking over of the St. John Valley Railway. I regard these two things as more important than any other matter of public construction in New Brunswick to be taken over. It would be relieving the province of a burden and tdoing a real good to the people. I am not quite so narrow in my political views that I would want to withhold credit from any administration that would grapple with these questions in a businesslike way. If these things were done, I would unhesitatingly say it was a good thing to do them, and that the administration which had done them was entitled to credit for doing them.

As I have already said, this amount is considered sufficient for any unforeseen conditions that may arise.
{Mr. J. H. King.]
It does not, however, take into account the transfer of these wharves. That is a matter of government policy, and must first receive the consideration of the government. After consideration has been given, if it is decided to take them over, an item could very properly be included in the Supplementaries.

May I ask the minister
this? Is it his intention to have the matter disposed of before the Supplementaries are down? It seems to me a question of that, or else of putting a blanket vote here that would be large enough to cover the cost. I would be glad to have the minister's assurance that the matter will be settled before the Supplementaries come down.

The matter has been held in abeyance for three or four years now. I hope that it will receive consideration from the government shortly, but as to the outcome I am not in a position to speak at tl^e present time.

What is the minister's own
attitude?

Is there any generally recognized basis for the granting of money for harbours, wharves and breakwaters? The reason I ask is this: I understand that at some of the ports in New Brunswick, St. John, for instance, there is a harbour commission.
Mr. -KING (Kootenay): Not at St. John.

We have harbour commissions controlling a good many of the harbours in Canada, and as I understand it, they do not get any grant from this parliament; they are supposed to be self-supporting. Is it right that we should grant hundreds of thousands of dollars to certain harbours while other harbours have to be self-supporting?

We have harbour commissioners in various parts of the country, more particularly at the larger ports. Some of the ports are self-sustaining, such as Montreal and Vancouver. With others, it is merely a matter of control. Some of the commissioners are paid officials, and some are not. There is no fixed principle applied throughout. Some of the harbours are self-supporting and provide moneys for improvements and repairs out of the tolls collected.- Others again, are dependent on the grants received from this parliament.
Are there any tolls collected from the vessels using these harbours for which we are making grants to-day?

I am not Bure. There are wharfingers at some of these wharves.

Supply-Public. Works
I imagine. These wharves have been turned over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and they would have knowledge of the tolls collected.
Is there any toll on coal shipped over the Joggin's wharf?
We have no information in our department regarding that. That would be in the Marine department.

What strikes me, in looking over the estimates for harbour and river improvements, is that the minister is asking for more money than he will require. The committee must bear in mind that this expenditure is spread very generally over Canada. Three of the western provinces get very little of it, I refer particularly to the item which is included for each of the provinces.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Harbours and rivers.

Under "Harbours and
rivers generally" the amount for Manitoba is only $15,000, and for the two provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta only $20,000, or $10,000 each. Large amounts are granted for the other provinces. Last year the sum of $60,000 was granted under this vote for Nova Scotia, and the minister says $46,000 was spent. For Prince Edward Island last year $14,000 was granted under this item, and two thousand odd was spent. For New Brunswick $65,000 was voted last year and some $11,000 was spent; and I assume that probably the same proportion will be maintained for the other provinces. There remains in the case of each province a large amount of this money unexpended, which is all to the good and to the credit of the Dominion and the minister, but the point is this: If the minister does not require more than one-half or say one-quarter of this amount why vote it, why put it in the estimates? It will only be a few days, or a few weeks at most, before the Minister of Finance comes to parliament with his budget. He will then tell the House "The Estimates amount to so much, I must raise a certain amount of money, and I must do it by taxation." In the meantime we are voting money-without very much inquiry, I grant-voting money that according to the record of last year was not spent-not nearly all spent. Now, would not the minister think it wise, under these circumstances, to revise these figures for harbours and rivers generally? If the amount is not required there is no use passing, it now. If we pass it now the plea will be, "There is the amount required and the taxes to meet it must be imposed." I should think it would be in the interest not only of the minister
and his department but of the country generally if we would cut these votes for harbours and rivers in each of the provinces by one-third, or even one-half. If an emergency arose, if some storm came up suddenly and washed away a wharf, or something of that kind, during the year the government could always get money, they did it last year; they could get it under Governor General's warrant. But if we vote money, as we propose to vote it now, it has to be made up when the budget comes down and has to be made up out of taxes. I think the minister would do well to reduce this amount.

In reply to my hon. friend I cannot quite follow his reasoning when he complains that we are not building more wharves and more piers in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. If my hon. friend has travelled across western Canada he will know that the requirements in those provinces for piers and wharves are not very great.
I made no complaint of that kind. I said those provinces get very little out of this large amount of money.
That is very true. Naturally they do not require a large expenditure.
I understand that.

As for the vote, as has been stated before, it is a contingency vote to be used for unforeseen expenditures. As I have already shown the committee the items that make up the total expenditure under this vote are very small in amount, and the suggestion that the minister, or the department should go to the Governor in Council for an order in council for five or six hundred dollars each time an expenditure on a wharf were required would not, I think, meet the approval of the committee. This is the usual vote and it is very necessary to the department to have it. The money is expended with care. As shown by the reports this year when expenditures have not been required they have not been made. I am satisfied, therefore, the committee will be well advised in leaving the estimate as it is. I can assure hon. members that there will be no extravagance in the expenditures, but the money will be there for the use of the department if it is required in the public interest.

The minister has entirely missed the point of what I said, or intended to say. I did not suggest that there was extravagance in the expenditure, nor did 1
Supply-Public Works

suggest that some vote was not necessary. What I did suggest was, that in view of last year's experience too much money was asked for, I said, lop off one-third or lop off one-half. I cannot see what justification the minister has for asking these large amounts when, according to his own showing, much smaller amounts were necessary last year. I made no suggestion that he is running to the Governor in Council for orders in council to authorize small expenditures-nothing of the kind. I said there was no danger in passing an estimate for a smaller amount because, if storms should arise and cause damage or difficulty occur it was always within his power to provide for such emergencies by a Governor General's warrant. I made no suggestion that he run with an order in council every time he wanted a few hundred dollars; but in regard to the order in council question there is this to be said-that with respect to an item of $85,000 that we have just passed he did proceed, without the authority of this parliament, on the strength of an order in council notwithstanding that he and his colleagues when in opposition so roundly denounced that particular course.

(Kootenay): In Kent county.

The work to be done is the tearing down of the present crib-tvork at low water level and building a concrete wall all round, building a concrete floor on the top of the wharf, and repairing the road leading to the wharf. The estimated total expenditure is $2,700.

Explanation.

Item agreed to.
Contrecceur-reconstruction of wharf headblock, $5,500.
Mr. STEVENS; I have asked the minister two or three times if he would spare us the necessity of asking questions. There is no explanation as to what this item is for. I think we should have an explanation of the new items. Was there a tender called for the $5,500? Is it to be done by day work?

It consists in removing all the decayed timber of the crib down to extreme low water level, building reinforced concrete wall 4 feet 6 inches at the base, 20 inches at the top, all around the headblock, and laying a 1-foot layer of concrete on the ice-breaker, and a 6-inch concrete flooring on the whole surface of the wharf. The total cost will be $5,000. It will probably be done by day work.

I understand the general policy of the government is that all work over $5,000'must, under the statute, be done by contract, but that does not necessarily mean that all work under $5,000 shall not be done by contract. Most of the items amounting to $3,000 or $3,500 could be done by contract to the advantage of the government.

I explained to the committee a little while ago that in the case of these repairs it is often difficult to let a contract. The work could be done more satisfactorily under a good foreman by day labour. If it is a renewal of work running over $5,000, the department in all cases, I think, try to have it done by contract, but in the case of repairs it is found they can be carried on better by day labour.

The minister pleads violation of the statute in such a simple form as that? The statute is there. To be told: why it is better to do it the other way, is only to be told that it is better to violate the statute. Why is it better? What is the difficulty in getting tenders for repair work on a wharf when the repair work runs to that sum? I do not see any difference be-

Supply-Public Works
tween the difficulty of the tender system as applied to repairs and as applied to renewals. To merely say that it is better is not any explanation to a fairly intelligent man.
I think the leader of the Opposition is familiar with the construction of a wharf.

Not very.
Mr. KING (Kootenay) = If he were, he would understand that when you undertake to tear down and remove, or to repair, a wharf, you never know what you are going to find. You may think it is only a small job, and when you get into the interior of the wharf you find the decay has gone further than you expected, and that is the reason why it is better to do the repairs under a competent foreman by day labour. It is hard to estimate what the work will cost until you start to take down the structure.
Do you intend to recommend an amendment to the statute, or just to violate it and let it go?
I am advised we have a right to do it under the statute.
There are certain conditions that have to be lived up to. Does the minister intend to try to live up to them?
We will try to live up to them.
Does the minister know what the conditions are?
If it is shown the work can be done more efficiently and more economically by the department, we have, I understand, the right to carry it on in that way.
That is subject to certain conditions. I am asking what those conditions are.
I think those are the conditions.

Oh, no. Does the minister want to tell us that when we have a statute saying that in all cases where the expenditure is over $5,000 the work shall be done by tender, it is all right for the minister to do it in some other way if he thinks fit? If that is the statute, I think he should introduce an amendment. But that is not the statute. There are some conditions. The minister should know them. I do not know them as I was never in that department, but I remember a discussion and a statement to the
effect that there is some provision whereby the reasons must be set out and must in some way be made known to parliament. I am asking that those conditions should be lived up to.

I think that is the condition. I think I have shown, in regard to this repair work, that it is very difficult to estimate and to know the cost and to let contracts, and in the discretion of the minister we have the right to carry on this expenditure by day labour, if we think it can be done more efficiently and more economically than by tender and contract.

Will the minister give the committee again what is intended by this vote. If he will do so, it will show, I think, very distinctly that his argument does not apply at all. It will show, if I recall it, the construction of a concrete wall and certain other specific works, and the item as it stands is not a repair; it is the reconstruction of a wharf headblock, an absolute work in itself, and certainly should be done by tender and contract. Will the minister be good enough to give the committee, in the light of his rather involved explanation of the statute, the explanation of this item?

The engineer advised the department that in his opinion this work could be done more economically by day labour. We have not made up our minds in regard to asking for an estimate for the work. I am not in a position to say that tenders will be asked for, but the recommendation of the district engineer is that this work can be done more efficiently and economically by day labour than by contract.

We should know the reason the engineer gave. On the face of it this is reconstruction and not repair. This is the reconstruction of a wharf, taking the old one down and putting up another. The reason the minister gives in the case of repairs would not apply at all. Just to be told that the engineer says so is not helping the committee. We might as well go home and allow the engineer to run the department with out the review of parliament.
Could the minister give us the engineer's report. He will have it under his hand.
I do not think 1 have that recommendation here, but I am told that that is his recommendation.

Could the minister give us the engineer's recommendation-his reason?
Sup-ply-Public Works

Give us his whole report, so that we can understand it.
I have not any reasons, as far as that is concerned. The engineer reported to me that that was one of the works he suggested could be done more economically by day work than by tender.

I think the item should stand till we find out what policy the department has followed. Surely the department reviews the reasons of the engineer, and surely this committee should review these reasons in a case where the committee feels that, on the face of it, there appears no reason in the world for departing from the statutory system. All we have been told, after a long series of inquiries, is that the engineer says we had better not follow the statute and had better do the work by day labour. Each question brings the same answer-"This is one of the cases where the engineer says so." What is the committee for?

I might ask:
What is the engineer for?

He is there to give his
reasons to the minister, and the minister is here to give them to the committee.

The duty of the
engineer is to advise the department as to these expenditures, and it is supposed that he is qualified. If not, he should be. On a matter of this kind the department and the minister would naturally accept his advice, unless it was found at times that the engineer was in error or was not carrying on the work properly. As regards the suggestion that the department had adopted a new policy, that is not true. This House has been voting similar supply for many years, and the same manner of departmental treatment has been going on. I do not think we are outside of the statute; I am advised that we are not and that, under the statute, we have power to make expenditures of that character. There is no objection, so far as I can see, to calling for tenders on these items, if the committee should so wish.

If the minister will
assure us of that, that will be satisfactory. The minister asks: "What is the engineer for?" The engineer is there to give his recommendations and his reasons therefor. Ht is the duty of the minister and his deputy to review them and the duty of the minister to give them In the House when they are asked for. If we are here only to hear that the engineer advises this or that, we are superfluous. We cannot deal with every case; but surely this is a case IMr. Stevens.]
which calls for some explanation, and the minister can give the reasons set forth by the engineer. The recommendation of the engineer in this case might, be all right, but we have a right to know what is back of the engineer's recommendation.

I have had a good deal

The recommendation does not comply with the statutes at all. The Public Works Act, section 36, has three subsections. The first part of the section provides that all contracts shall be let by tender. Then there are certain exceptions:
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest.
It is hardily suggested that this is one of those cases. I presume the minister claims to come in under (b):
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
Does he mean to say that he is going to do this by the officers and servants of the department?
Yes.

Does the hon. member
suggest that that permits day labour and the hiring of men to get the work done?
Yes.

I think a reading of the next subsection will make it clear that the section does not so permit. Subsection (c):
-where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
There the minister is enabled to get the work done by day labour. But if the cost is over five thousand dollars he can only do the work by the officers and servants of the de* partment That is certainly the intention of section 36. This work runs over five thousand dollars, and if the minister is not -in a position to do it by the officers and servants of the department he must do it by tender. Undoubtedly this means the regular officers and servants. If you say it means every one you

want to employ for this special work, then under that interpretation the whole section is gone. It means work in Ottawa where they have officers and servants already in the service of the department; then they can do it even if it is over five thousand dollars. If it is under five thousand dollars he has wider discretion, but when over that amount he is not allowed to go out and simply hire anybody he wants to get that work performed.

Exception number two
does not mean that the officials of this department can go down to the province of Quebec or of Nova Scotia or anywhere else and hire men themselves. They get the work done under foremen. For instance, they have a public works office in the city of Halifax, and I presume they have one or two in each province, and the work is done directly under the supervision of the department's engineers who visit various places where public works are in course of construction. In Nova Scotia there are probably ten engineers whose duty it is to supervise every bit of construction which is let without tender and contract, and in that way I think the minister may come in under subsection 2 of clause 2 of the exceptions, when the work will be done under the supervision of the department's officers.
The hon. member's interpretation simply repeals the section.
Oh, no.

I should like to know what is left of the section if the minister can simply say to an engineer, "Hire all the men you like and go to work and do that by day labour." If he can still do that, there is no section left. That is not the meaning of the section at all. The section permits the minister, when the work is under five thousand dollars, to do the work by the officers and servants of the department provided the minister takes the responsibility because owing to the nature of the work he thinks it advisable to do it in that way; but if the cost of the work is over five thousand dollars it must be done by tender, unless it can be done, not under, but by, the "officers and servants of the department." The meaning must be the regular officers and servants of the department, not those employed for the special purpose of doing the work. If they are so employed, and that interpretation is accepted, the section is nothing more or less than a farce.

Surely the right hon. gentleman does not take the ground that subsection 2 only provides for such work being done

In order that the minister may be on his guard I would like to point out that, whether intentionally or not I do not know, the recommendation of the engineer does not comply with the statute. The object of the law, which has been on our statute book for a long time, is as far as possible to enforce the system of tender and contract, the method of public competition, in connection with these works. A clause was inserted providing that in the case of all works in connection with which the cost exceeded $5,000, the system of tender and contract should be followed.
With certain exceptions.

Except in the case of the exceptions noted, and the engineer in this case is evidently trying to come within the language of the second of these exceptions. He has reported to the minister, on an unsigned report made by Mr. Cameron, I understand, that the work can be more advantageously done by day labour. Well, that is not what the statute asks him to certify. The statute says that the work shall be done by contract except in cases, in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department. There is nothing in it about day labour.
That is all right.

The minister says it is all right, but I may tell him that when the statute prescribes a certain line of action which must be followed unless certain things happen, those things which happen must come within the language of the statute. The engineer must certify that the work can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department, and I point out to the minister that his engineer has not so certified.

I am not advocating the violation of the law which declares that where the work will exceed $5,000 tenders should be
called for, but if we are doing this we are simply following the lines of the opposition when they were in the government, when Mr. Ballantyne was permitted to build his government merchant marine or a large number 'of those vessels, running into millions of dollars, without any tenders at all being called for.

The hon. member knows better than that. They were not under the Public Works Act to begin with. They were built in strict conformity with the item which parliament passed authorizing them to be built, and furthermore, were built in the only way they could be built. Anybody knows you could not possibly submit to tender the building of vessels like that, owing to the difference in the facilities of the various docks in this country, and besides, in no country in the world are vessels of that character or vessels of any character built by tender, neither in the United States nor in Great Britain; and that by means of the method adopted there and the conditions that were imposed the vessels were- built on an equality as to price with even those built in Great Britain, built in Scotland on the Clyde, and built at $20 per ton less than vessels of inferior quality were built for at the same time in the United States. The point is this: They could not have been built in any other way. The conditions did not permit it; the act did not call for it. The authority of parliament was strictly complied with in every regard. But in this case we claim that the authority of parliament is not complied with.
How much money was saved to the country by building those ships under that system?

About $20 per ton on sixty-three vessels; the hon. member can compute it for himself. It would amount to many millions, and what is more, they were well built. We are not in the position of the United States to-day of having them up for repair on account of poor construction. The reports show that every one of them was well constructed, and at an average of $20 per ton less than theirs which were poorly constructed. There has not been a better piece of work done by this country in so far as cheapness of construction is concerned.
They all went to pieces on the first opportunity.

Practically half a dozen of them are now at the bottom of the sea, due, it is claimed, to faulty construction.

On this item, when the minister makes his very general statement, I think it would be well for him to bring instances in support of it. If there was, I would like the minister to bring it forward, and not take refuge behind a Very general assertion. As long as he does that, I take no exception at all. It is not, of course, an argument to say when you are violating the law, that it has been violated before. If the minister thinks that, he should have the law amended. We do not object to ordinary repairs being done that way. Ordinary repairs come under $5,000 almost always.

We are not trying to harass the minister, but if we are going to say any time the minister tells us "The engineer told us to do it this way, that is enough for the committee," all well and good. This matter has been under the consideration of the department, I think, for some time. The district engineer reports on the subject as follows:
There is no deep water wharf between Batiscan and Quebec; all the wharves in this section are tidal wharves. Therefore it is absolutely important, if not imperative, to have a deep water wharf at this place, for the accommodation of the public, and to facilitate the importation of this important district.
At the present the steamer Etoile, plying between Montreal and Quebec, and the steamer St. Croix, plying between Quebec and St. Jean Deschaillons, land at Grondines when the water is sufficiently high, but do not stop when the water is too low. By this fact, the exporters are never sure whether the boat will stop or not, and very often, this is a cause of serious losses for them when their shipments consist in perishable merchandise such as cheese, butter, meat, etc.
The parishes interested in the general traffic of the proposed wharf are, St. Ubald, St. Marc, St. Alban, St. Thuribe, St. Casimir and Grondines, representing a total population of about 8,500 inhabitants. The welfare of the trade and commerce, and the general production to the above mentioned places depend on the shipping facilities and accommodation by water.
The exports consist of farm and dairy products, meat, vegetables and general merchandise, etc., which may average when a deep water wharf is built, from 3,500 to 4,000 tons per season.
The imports consist of the necessities of life for the above-mentioned population, and average 20 tons per week, but will increase considerably when the deep water wharf is built.
The proposed deep water wharf is a public necessity, and if not built, it would be most detrimental to the general production of this community.
That is the report we have from our district engineer on the advisability and the necessity for this wharf.

ing into a work of some significance, involving a very large expenditure of public money, at a time when we were all assured in this House and in the newspapers that this economic government was not launching on any large or any new expenditures for public works.
