No.
What is the amount?

That is one of the figures I mentioned. I fancy $150,000 will likely be next year's figures, but taking $130,000, that is ten times the amount, that was voted last year. Why should we have to ask for something that the minister obviously should tell the House? If he does not tell the House, the House is misled. The House had no reason in the world to assume that that was the commencement of an undertaking that would cost $130,000.

I do not know just why hon. members opposite will inject into the discussion to-day a debate which occupied the attention of this House time and again, and which I think, all fair-minded people will agree was settled without any discredit whatever to the then government. As a matter of fact, this discussion took place in the House on two or three occasions. My hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), the hon. Speaker of the House (Mr. Lemieux) then, a very prominent member of the opposition, my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), I think, and two or three other very prominent members on the other side of the House, commended the government. The former leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) was a member of the government when the contract was entered into. The war was proceeding at the time. The only possible reflection, or excuse for a reflection, upon that Contract was that the war collapsed, and because the war collapsed sooner than people expected the ships were not then as much needed as when the government undertook their construction.
Is it not a fact that the contracts for those ships were let after the war?
Every one of those contracts was let before the conclusion of the war.
The hon. member is absolutely wrong.

It is true the construction of ah the boats was not commenced until after the conclusion of the war; of that there is no doubt, but that has nothing to do with the question before the House at the present time. If we are going to have a debate on that whole question, let us have the debate with
all the facts before us. Let us discuss the important question if it is necessary to do so, but to raise a remnant, in a distorted fashion, of a debate held two or three or four sessions ago, in order to protect the minister on the item we are discussing to-day, and discussing, I think, in a fair manner without any intentional recrimination of any kind, I think is very poor tactics indeed. Now in regard to this item we have before us, the House was asked for a vote of $12,000. No explanation, as far as we can learn, was given to the House at the time. The minister replies "Well, I do not remember any explanation being asked for." Three or four times this afternoon I have had to suggest to the minister, in the most courteous possible way, that he should give to the House as we go along a general outline of what these new items are for. The minister did not give an explanation unless we persisted in asking for it. We were quite willing to facilitate the passing of the estimates; but now we are confronted with what certainly appears, I think, like a lack of courtesy to the committee. That is what occurred last year, and we do not know but what in these items which we have been passing, similar incidents will occur or will be discovered next year. The minister should certainly give the committee a more complete explanation of this appropriation than he has already done. There is a contract for $15,000. Will the minister explain what the contract is and what portion of the work is included in that contract?

I think I was quite justified
in making a comparison between the way in which this government was letting those contracts or doing the work and that of the old government. The leader of the Opposition * brought the matter up. We on this side of the House did not bring it up.
The hon. member's hon. friend across the floor brought it up.

The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) made the remark that all the contracts for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine were made when the Hon. Mr. Ballantyne brought down his first estimates.
I did not say that at all.
What did the hon. member say? That is exactly what he said.
No, I did not.

The hon. member said that all the money was voted and the contracts let and brought down when the first vote was asked for.

Supply-Public Works
I made no such statement.

The truth is that the last contract was made in 1920 and the first vote was asked for in 1918. It seems to me that there is absolutely no difference except that on that occasion the total amount was $80,000,000, and the total cost of this work is $130,000.
I do not like, when I am chasing a bear, to be diverted by a rabbit trail-
My right hon. friend would run from a bear.
But in this case the distinction is important to the House.
He would scare the bear.

I do not want any member of the House to feel that I am saying that in bringing down every estimate, you should bring down the whole amount required to complete the work for which that estimate provides. I am not saying that at all. The invariable practice of parliament has been to bring down the amount required for the year, but to state to parliament the total commitment the government is entering upon, toward which this is a contribution. In the case of , the mercantile marine the government came down in 1918 with a programme for a certain construction and not for the whole amount of money required for that construction. The government got the amount of money required, told parliament exactly the number of vessels, the tonnage and the estimated cost. Then in 1919, the government deciding on an extension of that, got the unanimous approval of parliament, without a single criticism, for a further programme and secured the vote required for expenditure that year. In 1920, there was some little objection; but the great row was raised in 1921, when the vessels were nearly completed, no further contracts being asked for, and no further programme, but merely a completion of what parliament had unanimously agreed to. What I am emphasizing is this: In every case the government told parliament the whole commitment into which parliament was entering when asking for the amount that would be required for that year.
I am complaining that the minister did not do that last year. It is impossible now to remedy that default; but I would impress this on the minister, that he should never come to parliament and let the House assume that that is all the commitment of the country that we are entering into in relation to' that estimate, merely taking refuge under the fact that no

question was asked. It is his duty to let parliament know the significance of an estimate. I ask the minister if that is not reasonable. I am prepared to let this go if the minister will agree to that. He should let parliament know the significance of an estimate whether questioned or not.

I quite agree with my hon. friend. That is true. The expenditure, last year, of $12,000, with the $15,000 tenders received, will construct the first section of this wharf. The additional sum asked is to carry on and continue another section. This is a large structure. We did not go beyond our authority in the vote given us last year. I quite agree with my right hon. friend that it would have been better-and I would have done so if the matter had occurred to me-to have informed the committee as to the commitment.

Let me read to the committee what occurred last year when these estimates were up:
Harbours and Rivers, Quebec-$236,785.
Sir Henry Drayton: Just one question. I take it from what my right hon. friend has said that these are for essential repairs. You are not going on with new works?
Mr. Mackenzie King: There may be one or two very small exceptions, but the votes would be for work that has been long standing and should really have been undertaken before this.
Sir Henry Drayton: There are some extensions here- $32,000.
Mr. King (Kootenay): Not extensions, but necessary additions. It is not new work.

Item agreed to.
The opening was there for the explanation; the request for information was all there, and yet that was the answer-that no new work was being undertaken, no extensions, but just ordinary repairs.
Is that the $1?,000 item?

That is the item included in the supplementary estimates.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering the item on page 37 of the Estimates, Grondines wharf, $50,000. Shall the item carry?

The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) had the floor at six o'clock. I think he intended to make some severe strictures on the government in connection with this item.

Supply-Public Works
I suggest we let the item stand for the present.

I find the minister was right in stating that last year the item of $12,000 for this wharf did not come up in the supplementary estimates. Unfortunately the supplementary estimates for harbours and rivers, Quebec, amounting to $236,785 went through with very, very little discussion, but what discussion did take place would certainly lead one to believe that no new works of any importance were contemplated by the government. The discussion will be found at page 3545 of the Hansard of last session. The item was called in the lump sum, and the discussion was as follows:
Sir Henry Drayton: Just one question. I take it from what my right hon. friend has said that these are for essential repairs. You are not going on with new works ?
Mr. Mackenzie King: There may be one or two very small- exceptions, but the votes would be for work that has been long standing and should really have been undertaken before this.
Sir Henry Drayton: There are some extensions here- $32,000.	.
Mr. King (Kootenay): Not extensions, but necessary additions. It is not new work.
Item agreed to.
What item were we referring to then?

The whole item in the
supplementary estimates for harbours and rivers, Quebec, involving a total of $236,785, tfie particulars of which are to be found at page 9 of the supplementary estimates of last session. In that list is the item of $12,006 for this particular wharf. ' I submit, Mr. Chairman, that when that item came before the House last session with the practical assurance of the Prime Minister, who happened to be in the chamber at the time, that no new works of any importance would be undertaken, any one then present would naturally conclude that this was one of the small works in his contemplation when he replied to my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), or that it was merely a repair or extension of some old work. There was nothing in the information given to the committee by the Minister of Public Works, there was nothing afforded by the discussion, to lead us to believe that we were launching on a work of considerable magnitude. I am not in a position to judge whether this work is or is not a proper work for the locality. I heard the statement from the minister this afternoon that it would serve a scattered population of about 8,500.
61J
I made the statement that it would serve an agricultural population of 8,500.
Well, if it is an agricultural population I may assume it must be a more or less scattered population. It is not a population contained in a town or city.
No.

To serve that community of 8,500 a proposal such as we had last session to expend $12,000 would certainly not be inappropriate. I am inclined to think that when the minister brought down his estimate last session he himself felt that $12,000 would be about the right amount for a wharf for that community. After having obtained the authority of parliament to expend that money, in the interval he has let a contract for $15,000 for this work, which is not very far wide of the mark; but he comes to parliament this session with the first information we get on the subject, namely, that the work is or soon will be under construction and will cost in the neighborhood of $130,000. That is a large expenditure for a government that announced that it was . not going to spend large sums on new works. It may be a proper expenditure; I am not in a position to judge that, but the manner in which the vote was passed last year could hardly be called a proper one. Hon. members are entitled to be given the facts in regard to these matters; surely the committee is entitled to know what is in the minister's mind when he launches a proposal of this kind. If, as I believe, the minister contemplated last session an expenditure of only $12,000 on this work, his course to-day should be to say so rather than to put in $50,000 for this year and then say that the ultimate cost is to be about $130,000. We know that these estimates are generally overrun; in all probability even that proposed expenditure will be increased by another 25 per cent for additions, extras, and the like, before the work is completed. I want to register my protest in respect to the manner in which this matter was brought before the House and dealt with last session, without a single particle of information to enable us to judge whether we were voting correctly or incorrectly or whether we were spending money wisely or unwisely. I have no desire in any away to reflect on the minister in 'this matter, but I do not want to see such a system gain ground in this House, and in order to make my protest as strong as I can I propose to move that this item be reduced to the sum of $15,000, which is the amount for which I understand, a contract has been let.
Supply-Public Works

I quite agree, as I did this afternoon, with the statement of the right hon. leader of the Opposition that an explanation should have been given to parliament last year, but in the rush that took place the statement was not made. Not one dollar of the $12,000 that was voted last year has been spent. A contract has been let. It is in the province of the government to cancel it and pay damages to the contractor. But we are in a position to-day to give the explanation that shotdd have been given last year; in fact, I did give it this afternoon. This work is important to the community it will serve, and the government believes it is justified in asking parliament now for another $50,000 with which to proceed with it. Nothing having been so far expended, the whole matter is open for discussion and review, but from the reports we have in the department I submit that this is a necessary public work and that it should receive the support of parliament.

I do not dispute that the work may be of use, but is there no relationship between use and cost? At first sight, passing by entirely the question of the way the vote was obtained last year and accepting the minister's statement that it was not obtained in the proper way, that is to say-
I did not state that.

I do not mean improper in the moral sense, but that it was not obtained in the right way; an explanation should have been given and the facts made known to the House. I accept the minister's statement in that regard and pass it over. But on the surface it does not look justifiable to have a $130,000 wharf when, according to the minister's own statement, there are only
8,500	people in the community it will serve, and they not engaged in anything that particularly requires ocean transport. I do not say that the community does not require a wharf; no doubt it does. But the amount suggested is about $13 or $15 per head for the wharf alone. If the minister goes on that principle, how much is it going to cost to string the whole province with wharves? Will the minister make it clear just what facilities these people have now? What have they been doing all along to get their produce to market? What is going to be the saving to them per annum on account of the wharf being built, taking into account, of course, the fact that they will still be at some expense? Will the

minister tell the circumstances as they exist without the wharf and then state the advantages that are expected to accrue to that small number of people from the building of it?

I think I gave the information to the committee this afternoon. My hon. friend speaks of 8,500 people. It is true that it is an agricultural community, the shipments from it being largely the products of the farm. They are a great distance from their markets, Quebec and Montreal. They have been using a wharf which serves at certain heights of water, and it is proposed to build a wharf that will afford them communication with these large centres during the summer season. We have investigated the matter very carefully since last session and we are satisfied that the proposed expenditure is a proper one.

Mr. Chairman, before the vote is taken on the motion of the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), I wish, as a member for one of the ridings of the Quebec district, to express my great astonishment at the sense of economy displayed by the ex-Minister of Militia just at a time when it is proposed to carry out public works in the province of Quebec. I should have liked, and I think the majority of the members of this committee are also of the same opinion, that this sense of economy, no doubt inspired by the public interest, should have rather existed in the hon. member at the time of the general elections in 1921. Indeed, very large contracts suddenly became necessary in the riding of the hon. member at the last general election, and, if I am not mistaken, a sum of almost $50,000 was spent during the campaign so as to enable the hon. member to further represent his electors. I might suggest to the hon. member not to try and economize always at the expense of the same people, but to allow the government to make the expenditures which are actually needed. Grondines is one of the most flourishing parishes of the beautiful county of Portneuf, and if the hon. member for Wellington were to visit that place I have no doubt that he would be the first to withdraw his objections. Those places are highly populated and prosperous, they are parishes where the wharves are of the greatest usefulness and all expenditure made there at present is in the interest of the public. Certainly, like the hon. member, I favour & sound economy, but economy in the public interest is part of a reasonable and sound policy, and it would be useless for the government to try and practise economy

Supply-Public Works
by not spending a few thousand dollars where it is necessary to keep in repairs wharves for which large sums have been spent. I think the hon. member could, during the present session, practise his sense of economy to a greater advantage if he proposed, for instance, to decrease the expenditures which are made in the harbour of Toronto, where there will never exist a satisfactory harbour, rather than oppose expenditures on public works in the province of Quebec, for the parishes bordering the St. Lawrence river, where the wharves, as I mentioned a few moments ago, are necessary and useful and where this expenditure will evidently be for the public welfare.
Has the hon. member persuaded the minister to give us the information we asked for?
I hope my right hon. friend is now convinced that this public work is a necessity.

I am sorry that I could not follow my hon. friend for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) in the remarks which he has just made, but this I was able to gather, that he is in some way or other under the impression that my objection to this particular item was that 'it pertained to the province of Quebec, and I think he said it would be better if I directed my attention to Ontario.
The only criticism I have offered on these estimates so far has been in respect of the harbour improvements generally in the Maritime provinces. I am not objecting to the item as an item, nor do I regard the fact as important whether it applies to Quebec or any other province. What I am objecting to is the principle. I am afraid that a system may grow up or is growing up whereby a minister or a government can pass an insignificant vote through parliament and start some considerable work, and then come back to parliament the following year and ask for more money to carry on the work, whereas had parliament had full knowledge of the situation when the first vote was asked it might never have been authorized. The same thing applies to half-a-dozen items we have passed this afternoon for public works. They are evidently new works. Nothing was voted for them last year. We have passed them in the belief that the two or three or four or five thousand dollars which is presented in the estimates was the final amount required. Now it may be that some of these items are only the entering wedge, the beginning of a heavy expenditure.
What I wish to point out particularly is this, that if the minister at the time he brings in his estimates has in contemplation the expenditure of a large sum of money on any public work, he should first make the facts known to the House when he asks for the initial amount required. In this case that was not done. I am satisfied that in this case the House voted $12,000 last session believing that they were voting that sum for a wharf for this particular locality, and I believe it is news to every hon. member on this side of the House that the $12,000 was only the beginning of the matter and that it is going to cost at least 1130,000 before this wharf is in place. It matters not whether it is in Ontario or Quebec or any other part of Canada; the place is a matter of no consequence.
Is not the item under consideration Item No. 157?
No. It is Grondines wharf, $50,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The first item on page 38, resolution No. 157.
And that resolution covers the province.of Quebec.

I am only objecting to the first item at the top of page 38 of the Estimates. I am not criticising the other items. I am directing myself entirely to this one, and to a practice which has sprung up, and which I trust will not go any further. As I said in my opening remarks, it is to protest against that practice that I move that this vote be reduced.

If the hon. member objects to the principle involved in the vote of this money, and not to the particular item, why does he not move that this whole resolution for harbours and rivers be struck out? Then he would not be in the position of having the criticism made that he has selected a particular place in the province of Quebec and made that his target. .
He does not like Quebec or Nova Scotia.
Why does he not move to cut out the whole resolution? .
Because I do not think the whole of it is objectionable. I have agreed to pass item after item.
But it is a question of principle.

I do not think any one either in the government or outside can con-
Supply-Public Works

scientiously support this practice. The minister has to excuse it himself. He says the vote last year was rushed through in the last days of the session.
Did you not agree to it?

I did through ignorance because the information was not given me at the time. That is what I complain of. I say that the principle is a bad one. We have passed item after item to-day and the same thing may occur next year with regard to them. The minister may come back next year to say that parliament authorized these expenditures of two or three or four thousand dollars this year and that that was only the beginning. I know it is the practice of the department and has been for twenty-five years, whether the practice be good or bad, that when a vote for a public work passes this House the department goes ahead and lets contracts irrespective of the amount voted by parliament, the assumption being that the House has committed itself to the principle of the work, and if we vote ten or twenty or twenty-five thousand to-day the department will go ahead and let contracts for $100,000 or $150,000. That has been the practice for the last twenty-five years to my knowledge.

That has not been done in this case. If there is any objection to this particular item, the matter is in the power of this House. We have only let a contract for $15,000 on a vote of $12,000 passed last year. We have not abused our privileges. We have inquired into the matter and satisfied ourselves that this is a proper vote.
The minister will see this, that if on a vote of $12,000 you can let a contract for $15,000, surely the same reason applies and you could let a contract for $50,000 on the same vote.
But it was not done.

I know, but during the last twenty-five years it has been done time and time again on the assumption that when parliament votes the money it approves the work. Then the department goes ahead and carries out the work. If that is a good practice, and it always has been the practice in my time at least, then on each of these item3 for two or three or four thousand dollars, contracts might be let and new works undertaken and the House in the meantime have no knowledge of what the ultimate expenditure is going to be. W'hat I complain of is that what we did, we did in the dark. We should

have had the information. The minister should have come down to the House with a new proposal and candidly said: This is a new proposal to complete a work which will ultimately cost $130,000.

In answer to my hon. friend, who claims that this is a matter of principle and that his criticism is not applied to any particular province, I would draw his attention to this fact: Resolution No. 154 "Harbours and rivers" applies to Nova Scotia. This was passed without any objection, I understand, from my hon. friend.
Oh, no; it was not, I criticised it.

Resolution No. 155 "Harbours and 'rivers" applies to Prince Edward Island; resolution No. 156 "Harbours and rivers" applies to New Brunswick; resolution No. 157 "Harbours and rivers" applies to Quebec and is now under consideration. The most peculiar feature of the case, however, is this: My hon. friend professes a desire to protect a principle in the public interest, but his objection to the conduct of the Public Works department is only awakened or aroused when we reach this particular item No. 157 which covers public works in the province of Quebec. If my hon. friend really wishes to fight for a principle why does he not, as suggested by the hon. member (Mr. Power), move an amendment which would apply to all the items generally, so that a reduction of expenditure would be required in all cases and not simply in the case of the province of Quebec? If my' hon. friend does that he will have a better chance of making good his claim that he is fighting for a principle, and not merely trying to reduce public expenditure in the province of Quebec notwithstanding the smallness of the amount involved.
The hon. member for Dorchester is an intelligent man.
Thank you.

I do not think he could have been in the House for any very considerable length of time prior to six o'clock or he would not have made this address. I do not think it is worthy of him, endeavouring to make out of this instance a case of prejudice on the part of members of this House against his province.

If my right hon. friend will allow me, I am not trying to make a case, I am trying to help my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) to modify his position so as not to lend himself to misinterpretation.

Supply-Public Works

I want to assure the hon. member that when his ingenuity is applied to the creation of that misinterpretation, it would take a very skilful man indeed to find a method of avoiding it. He argues that because we apply our objection to this resolution 157 we are consequently animated by prejudice against his province. The objection raised, and the point has been conceded by the minister, was against the practice which developed only in this single instance applied not to resolution 157 but only one' item in it namely: the Grondines wharf. In relation to that the minister admitted that he obtained last year a vote of $12,000 without giving to parliament, or to the committee of parliament, the vital fact that the $12,000 was only for a commencement, and that the whole work would cost $130,000. The protest of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is against that fact. It has not been revealed that that practice was adopted-it may have been but it has not been revealed that it was -except in regard to this Grondines wharf and objection could not be applied to other items in resolution 157, or to resolutions 156 and 154; the ground of objection relates only to the one item. Objections in relation to the Nova Scotia estimates were taken on other grounds and protests were made. It is only in connection with this particular item that we object on the ground stated; and I find some hon. members, in more articulate and dignified form, or more frequently, protesting that we are prejudiced against Nova Scotia. How foolish this is. We object to such a practice. I must commend the minister. He was rather frank in the matter; he admitted it was not the right practice. I accept that statement and only hope it will not be repeated.

I have
personal knowledge of what took place when the item for this work was voted last year because I happened to occupy the Chair at that time. The item came up in the Supplementary Estimates in the closing days of the session, and with the exception of one or two questions the whole of the items were adopted without discussion of any kind. It has been the experience for many years when these things are done, that a certain amount is voted to begin the work, and the work is continued the year following, and so on, until the contract is completed. It has been suggested here over and over again that we might adopt a system, which I am told exists in England, by which when the estimates are prepared and a new work is undertaken a statement is made out showing the details of the work, what it will cost and so on, and
the members can see at a glance exactly how the matter stands. If members will look through Hansard in past years they will find that with respect to any particular item very little information is given unless a question has been put concerning it; and the estimates themselves only state the amount to be expended during the year, or the amount voted the year previous. Whether there should not be a change in our present system is a matter which is well worth consideration.
With respect to this particular item I can say with respect to Grondines, which is forty miles from Quebec, that there is there a tide of fifteen feet, and a twelve or fifteen thousand dollar wharf there is out of the question entirely. It is a place much frequented during the summer season by the market boats of Quebec, and by the boats running to the south shore of the St. Lawrence. It has a population of over 8,000 people and is one of the most productive districts situated near the city of Quebec. Not far from Grondines is Donnacona where there is now one of the largest pulp mills in the province. The district is developing very rapidly, and if anything of substantial value in the way of a wharf is to be provided at that particular point, we must construct a wharf that will stand. The tides of the St. Lawrence at that place are tremendous, and a twelve or fifteen thousand dollar wharf is out of the question there.

Does the pulp mill to
which my hon. friend has referred use this wharf ?

lit is a
benefit to the district I am told. Grondines is the nearest place to that settlement. As a result of the erection of the pulp mill the whole district is developing very considerably.

Will the pulp mill use
this wharf?

I cannot
state that, but I do know that the whole district has benefited very considerably from the erection of the mill in question. I think the committee should adopt this item on the assurance which the minister has given that the matter will be thoroughly investigated, and if the expenditure is not justified no other outlay will be involved except that under the contract now entered into. At a subsequent session, when a further amount will be necessary if the work is to be pursued, the committee with fuller information will be in a position to pass judgment on the matter. I think we should not hastily pronounce on it now with the limited information in our pos-
Supply-Public Works

session, especially when the minister has assured us that the whole matter will be thoroughly investigated.
With that understanding I have no objection to withdraw my amendment.

I think the manner in which this vote has been submitted to the House is wrong both in principle and in practice. However, the Minister of Public Works has admitted that it was not a right thing to do and I think we should accept his explanation. I would like to add that I believe the leader of the Opposition and the. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) have done a good service in bringing this matter to the attention of the committee. As I said before I believe it is a wrong practice. I can easily see where the principle might be abused and work carried on from year to year in an irregular manner, if the appropriations could be obtained in such a way without parliament being cognizant of all the facts. I should like very well if the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) would withdraw the amendment, because I will vote for the item as it stands in the estimates.
I will withdraw it.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw the atttention of the committee to the fact that this wharf will be built in the interest of the agricultural class. Not only the farmers of Grondines have signed a petition requesting the building of this wharf, but also those of the parishes of Deschambault, St. Gilbert, St. Marc des Carrieres, St. Casimir, St. Thuribe, St. Ubalde, and even those of Ste. Anne de la Perade in the adjoining county; as it is far more advantageous for the farmers to carry their products by water than by rail.
I reiterate my statement that the construction of this wharf will especially be to the advantage of the farmers and I express the hope that the committee will approve of this item.
Amendment withdrawn.

Item agreed to.
Grosse Rouche-wharf repairs, $3,500.
Is this a similar case to the other? I see the item is $3,500, and it was $1,350 last year. What is the estimated expenditure, and why was it not given when the vote was asked for last year?

The vote last year was for urgent repairs. We are completing a certain amount of work this year to renew
[Mr. Maroil.l
the superstructure of the wharf for the top three or four feet and paint the shed shelter and railing.
Was the work expected to be completed with the $1,350 last year?
No.
The House should have been informed on that point.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $75,000.
How much w7as spent of the $75,000 voted last year?
What was it spent on?
On small repairs to various structures throughout the province. It is a very long list.

What is the largest
item?
The items vary from $85 to $916.

Item agreed to.
La Malbaie-wharf, $12,000.
We should have some explanation of that. Is that in the same category as the Grondines wharf? It is a large sum.
No, I think not. This is for the construction of a crib and span wharf 299 feet long by 16 feet wide, including the headblock 24 feet by 36 feet.
Is the work under contract?
Yes, it is under contract?

Where is the wharf and what vessels use it?

Item agreed to.
L'Islet-wharf repairs, $23,500.

This is apparently a remarkable case. Last year the vote, without explanation too, was $1,500. Now the minister asks for $23,500. Why was parliament not informed that the appropriation involved this expenditure?

Last year, we made just small repairs to the flooring of the wharf. The report of the engineer this year would indicate that it is necessary to replace 80,000 feet of face timbers, 60,000 feet of cross ties, 15,000 feet of longitudinals, 65,000 feet of stringers, 100,000 feet of 3-inch flooring, and 500 square yards of gravel surface.
This is another case similar to those as regards which the minister told us a little while ago the work would be done by day labour. This is surely a work that should be done by contract.

Mr. Chairman, allow me to add a few remarks in regard to the vote for repairs to the wharf of L'lslet. It would astonish me if the House paid more attention to statements emanating from a member who resides hundreds, nay, thousands of miles distant from my county, rather than be guided by information which I can personally extend. The leader of the Opposition, just now, told us that the vote of $23,500 was a similar case to the one of $50,000 asked for on behalf of Grondines. Well, Sir. if parliament is called upon, to-day, to vote such a large sum, it is due to the fact that the government, while the leader of the Opposition was at the helm, neglected to carry out the necessary repairs to this wharf. The wharf at L'Islet dates back over a hundred years. It serves as a refuge harbour and is utilized by three or four hundred farmers. Goods to the amount pf a $1,000,000 consisting of farm products and lumber are carried over it each year. At present five parishes handle at this wharf both the products they ship and the goods they import. The public works could, I think, economize considerably, and, one of the first ways to do so would be to carry out the necessary work at the proper time and thereby not allow public property to deteriorate as it has unfortunately happened during a certain number of years, especially down on the lower St. Lawrence. One of the reasons why this work is so costly is that the government is obliged to buy its lumber in the summer season. If it was possible to have the
Supply-Public Works

lumber prepared by the farmers in winter, it would not only be an economy but at the same time a help to the rural class. Not only the present system of carrying out the work is of a more costly nature but it has for effect, in many cases, to delay the work for more than a year.
I sincerely regret that the majority of my hon. friends on the other side are not able to understand me; but I can assure them that my remarks have been made in a very good spirit, and that the money that will be voted for the wharf at L'Islet will be spent as economically as possible.

I have had a little experience in my part of the world as regards the construction of wharves, and I know the most costly wharf we have, one of very considerable proportions, cost from $12,000 to $15,000. Now we find an appropriation of $23,500 asked for, not for construction, but for repairs only. I should think that would not repair,
9 p.m. but construct a fairly large and very substantial wharf. We ought to know something of the size of this wharf, the nature of its construction, whether tenders have been called for and, if so, the amount of the tenders.

Matane harbour improvements, $100,000.

It must be apparent that hon. members should receive the very information which the minister gave us regarding the last item. I personally thank him for giving that information. It has an effect on me at once and I realize that the wharf at L'lslet is one of very considerable importance.
Carried.

This work of improving the harbour at Matane is of considerable importance, and it is surely not the desire of hon. members opposite that these items should be rushed through without any information being given.

I was on my feet about as soon as my hon. friend, with the intention of giving some information regarding this matter. This expenditure is required towards a fairly large project-the improvement of the harbour at Matane. It has been under the special study of an investigating board of five Public Works' engineers in charge of the assistant chief engineer on the understanding that if it were found practicable to build the harbour required we would ask for an estimate. The board of engineers have reported favourably. It is not a new project, it has been before the department for some years, but it has always been considered as a very large expenditure for the public benefit' to be gained. Representations were made again last year. They were not entertained. But during the interval between last session and this session one of the large would-be users of this proposed harbour-the Hammermill Paper Company who are operating large pulp limits in this district-advised the department that they were prepared to contribute practically 50 per cent of the cost.

Supply-Public Works
Matane is situated between Rimouski and Gaspe, a distance of about 150 miles, on a very bleak coast, and it is important that we have a harbour of refuge to accommodate that extensive coast line. Large undertakings in the way of fishing and lumbering are being carried on and there is a very heavy marine traffic on the river. Having received a bona fide proposition from the Hammermill Paper Company to pay to the government $10,000 a year for twelve years towards the cost of this work-estimated to amount to about $210,000-or to pay a lump sum of $100,000, we carefully investigated local conditions and fully considered the offer. As a result it is felt by the department and by the government that in the interests of the community at Matane and of the mariners who use the river, it would be good business for the people of Canada to supplement the cash offer and construct a harbour at Matane. Matane itself is a prosperous community.
What is it, a village or a town?

A small town of
3,500	people, but there is a scattered population throughout the parish of approximately 7,000. Large lumbering operations are being carried on in the district. The Hammermill Paper Company have a very large pulp mill at this point and intimate that they will carry on operations over a term of twenty or twenty-five years, paying in wages some $300,000 per annum. In addition to its local industries Matane is the base for the operations of the big pulp and paper companies on the north shore. The St. Lawrence broadens out at this point and there is a very large expanse of water down beyond Rimouski, so that it is very important for the men who earn their livelihood along this bleak coast line to have a harbour of refuge between Rimouski and Gaspe.
This matter has been carefully considered not only departmentally, but by the government and by special committee of council, and the government has reached the, conclusion that arrangements should be entered into with the Hammermill Paper Company and the work undertaken. So far as the company are concerned, they have already deposited $35,000 in cash and given a bond for the balance, the money to be paid over by them as the expenditure is made from time to time by the government.
There is no natural harbour at this point as I understand from the minister. Are the Hammermill Paper Company actually in operation?
Yes, the government have a harbour there. Last year $15,000 was voted for improvements, but this larger project having been put forward we have only expended $11,000 of that amount.
Was last year's the first expenditure for harbour improvements at this point?
The work has been going on for many years.
Will the minister give the committee an outline of the proposed new works?

There will be considerable dredging at the entrance to the channel, 134,000 cubic yards, estimated to cost $60,000; dredging at the turning basin, 155,000 cubic yards, estimated to cost $69,750; extension to eastern breakwater $40,320; dredging for crib seats, 1,000 cubic yards, estimated to cost $450; foundation crib for beacon, $2,550; crib work wharf connecting old wharf and western breakwater, $26,000; pile protection work, etc., $2,500. The total expenditure will amount to $201,875.

This item refers to work in my riding, Mr. Chairman, and I wish to add a little to the information which the hon. minister has so well conveyed to the committee. We have no place where vessels can shelter between Rimouski and Gaspe, and this has resulted in considerable loss of life and property year after year. The various companies operating on the north shore are: Ontario Paper Company at Franquelin, Shelter Bay and Maniquagan; North Eastern Pulp and Paper Company at Maniquagan, which has bought 3,000,000 acres of land and intends to build a pulp mill at a cost of between $6,000,000 and $7,000,000; Franquelin Lumber Company at Franquelin; St. Regis Paper Company at Godbout; Gulf Pulp and Paper Company at Clarke City, and H. F. Amory at Mingan. Several of these companies are waiting for the construction of this harbour in order that they may be able to bring their product across and ship it by rail from this point. The construction of this wharf will afford better transport facilities; it will increase the traffic of the Canadian National Railways as well as of the Canada and Gulf Terminal Railway. The minister has mentioned the Hammermill Company; I may say that Price Brothers are also operating at Matane and I know that Sir William Price himself is in favour of these harbour improvements. The minister has fully explained this vote and it it not necessary for me to repeat what he has said.

Mr. HANSON1: Is it intended to do any export business here, or will it be local traffic along and across the St. Lawrence?
It will accommodate both.
What export traffic will there be?
Pulpwood.
Price Brothers are exporting.

Is this expenditure dependent upon an agreement between the company and the department? In other words, is it stipulated that the company must pay $10,000 annually for twelve years as a condition of this vote? To what depth of water is the dredging to extend at low water? Was this work the result of a request by the company, or did the government itself feel that harbour improvements at that point were necessary? It is a little unusual that important works of this kind should be undertaken by the department at the instance of a company who, naturally, would want the work done for their own private, gain. I can appreciate, on the other hand, the fact that such work might be warranted on account of the magnitude of the proposed operations of the company.

I have been asking for improvements at that harbour since 1917; I have repeated my request every year, but have up to' now been unsuccessful. Petition after petition has been filed each year with the Department of Public Works, but without avail. These petitions were signed by the people of Matane, Ste. Felicite, St. Luc, St. Leandre, St. Ulric, and other communities whose merchants receive their goods through - Matane harbour. There is no proper accommodation for the vessels, and I have seen them at times riding at anchor six or seven abreast. It is high time that something was done to provide proper facilities at that harbour. I have endeavoured for years to have something done in this line, and I have finally succeeded in arranging for the payment of a certain sum by a company interested in development there. As my request year after year met with refusal, I came to the conclusion that if I could not get some assistance from other sources it would be impossible for me to succeed in the object I had in view. So I made a success of it, and I sincerely hope that the item will carry.

I am glad for my hon. friend's sake that he has at last found a sympathetic ear. I am not surprised to learn that he did his utmost to secure a grant in the past. For

some eight or ten years, being a supporter of the late government I made many similar requests on behalf of my riding, but as that government was a most economical one, I was unsuccessful, and I am not surprised that my hon. friend also was unsuccessful. It is quite evident now that he is making up for lost time, for he is getting a pretty good chunk. I should be glad, however, if the minister would give us the information we seek.

It is proposed to have a channel of a depth of nine feet at low water. A great deal of credit is due the hon. member for Matane (Mr. Pelletier) in the matter of securing a contribution from the Flammermill Company; it is due entirely to his efforts that this arrangement has been made. The government like to help those who help themselves. There are times-they rarely occur, of course-when an industry is so interested in development that it can be prevailed upon to contribute something toward the cost of a work like this. The hon. gentleman has succeeded in going much further than is usual in negotiations of this kind. The company will carry on extensive operations, and they believe that with proper harbour facilities their undertakings wTill be successful. The government are taking advantage of their offer and are supplementing their contribution with an equal sum. We believe the result will be to afford a harbour of refuge not only to the people of Matane, but to those of the surrounding country as well.
How much has been spent up to the present time on this harbour?
Over $121,000 has been expended since the inception of the harbour some years ago.

The minister stated that for many years it had been considered that this large expenditure would not be justified. The hon. member for the constituency makes a very strong plea respecting the need of refuge at this point. But has there not been a harbour there sufficient to give that accommodation to the people?
No.

The expenditure
seems very large, considering the depth to be obtained in the harbour-nine feet.
The present harbour could not afford refuge to the larger craft.

What is the depth now?

Supply-Public Works
Not more than four or five feet, I am advised.
Is it hardpan, rough bottom or mud?

I think it is mud-soft material.

The amount expended last year was S999. The present amount required is to renew 8,000 square feet of three-inch flooring.

I think the committee would like to have some information with regard to these various votes for wharves. I was not aware that there were so many ports in this particular locality. Would the minister give some information to the committee as to what the money is needed for as the items come up?

I shall be glad to give any information that is requested, but I do not want to block the work of the committee by interjecting unless it is necessary. What in the world is wrong with all these wharves? Are they all going to rack and ruin since my hon. friends opposite came into power? There are no less than forty-nine votes for wharf repairs or improvements, aggregating $572,785. What is the trouble? Why is it that so many of these wharves are needing attention all of a sudden?
We were in opposition before.

Point au Pic, Murray Bay-wharf repairs, $18,000.
Is this for the large pier at Murray Bay? Is that pier owned by the Dominion government?
Yes.
There must be a very considerable revenue from that wharf.
I have not the information as to the revenue. This work is owned by the Dominion government. Large steamers call at the pier.
Is it proposed to do this work by day labour or by contract?

Apparently we
have not received a recommendation from the engineer with regard to this work, so I am not in a position to say. It is a large amount, and evidently it would be preferable to have it done by contract.

I would think it would be preferable, but some works for which we have passed large amounts the engineer is evidently of the opinion should be done by day labour. Pointe a Elie-Magdalen Islands-wharf repairs and improvements, $5,850.

How much of last year's vote of $11,400 was spent? It looks to me as if these wharves were getting worn out very fast. I wonder if it is because of all the shells and boxes that are being moved over them.
The amount expended last year was $9,000.
And it is proposed to spend nearly $6,000 this year. What is in contemplation? Is there any more to follow next year?

I have no knowledge of that. Apparently they are trying to get the wharf into a state of repair. It is proposed to build a shed, and to extend the breastwork for a length of 150 feet, and to renew the stringers.
Is this work to be done by tender or day labour?

Item agreed to.
Pointe aux Trembles-wharf repairs, $15,200.

Is this one of those cases where a large undertaking was started without information being given to the House as to the ultimate cost? I do not think there should be much criticism of the previous item for repairs to the wharf in the Magdalen Islands, for anything we can do to better the condition of these people should be done, as they are very isolated. But that is not the case with the item under consideration. This is a very large amount. You must be rebuilding this wharf, or building two or three wharves, judging by the amount. You are spending $40,000 in two years. It does occur to me that some very considerable explanation ought to be given to the House as to why $25,000 was asked and probably spent last year, and why it is necessary to ask for almost as much again this year. The money is being largely wasted, I presume.

My hon. friend has not got that right. If he will look at the vote again he will find that we are asking for a revote of $15,200. The contract was let for $21,266 and there are contingencies, $2,234, making a total of $23,500. The probable expenditure for 1922-23 is $8,300 on the contract leaving a balance of $15,200 as the revote this year.
To complete the work?
Yes.
The vote last year was $25,000 for this. It is all marked for repairs?
Yes.

How could the repairs to a wharf cost $25,000. The wharves that have been brought to my attention, seemingly pretty -large ones, cost about half of that to build new. Is it not merely a re-constructed wharf?
It is not. .
It is not? How much has this wharf cost up to date, how much has been the capital cost to the country of this wharf up to the present time?
In June 1904 a contract was entered into for the construction at a cost of $33,775. The construction cost $32,944, and since that date $14,308.75 has been expended in repairs.
There has been $46,000 spent on it up to this new venture in repairs?
Yes.
Forty-six thousand and $25,000 more, seventy-one thousand odd dollars in capital cost outside- of interest. Now, will the minister tell us how much revenue has ever been collected from it?
I cannot tell, I have not the information. That might be secured, but these wharves are not revenue producing, as a rule, as my hon. friend knows.

I am not saying anything as to that now but I would like to know the exact situation. Commencement was made apparently in 1904 and up to now, including the repairs under way, it has cost $71,000. Could the minister not give us an approximate estimate of the revenue collected from that wharf?
The Department of Public Works would not know what the collections are. I will inquire from the Marine department what revenues they are collecting.
Would it amount to anything appreciable at all?
I do not think it.
Practically nothing.
Not very much I think.

Now, let me put this to the minister: Does he know of any reason why public works of this sort, that are utilized in trade, should not pay a reasonable interest on

Supply-Public Works
the cost? Does he know why they should not when, say, government elevators that are utilized in trade are compelled to pay interest on their cost? Will the minister explain the principle that distinguishes the one class from the other? What is the reason for applying one yard stick to one class and a different kind of yard stick to another?
I have no objection to my hon. friend making representations of that character. He knows well that his government-
I know that.

- did not advocate such a policy, and this government has not been carrying out a policy of that character either. It is a matter of policy. We know that in many of these country communities it would be subjecting the people to great hardship to collect wharfage charges for package freight.

I am very much interested in the minister's statement because our farmers in New Brunswick pay wharfage charges for loading their potatoes on the wharf at St. John, and I do not see why we should have to pay such charges if farmers in other places are not paying for the same service. In this connection, Mr Chairman, it is just possible I am hardly in' order, but due to the fact that I was serving on a committee which sat this afternoon I was not in the chamber when the estimates for New Brunswick were under consideration, and therefore I would ask the minister if it is proposed to bring down any estimate for the breakwater in St. John harbour called the Negro Point breakwater. This is a very great necessity. It is not, like some of the works we have had under consideration to-night, a local work. St. John is the winter port of the East for the whole shipping of Canada.
No, Halifax.

My hon. friend called attention to Halifax. Well, there is a little place called Halifax from which they ship a few apples. But I still contend that St. John is the winter port, not because it is a bigger place or that the harbour is possibly better than that of Halifax, but due to the fact that St. John is nearer the bulk of freight that is sent east for ocean shipment. We have a condition there of such a character that unless this breakwater is built we shall not benefit from the wharves constructed by the government. There is a dock already constructed, I think it is dock 17, on which there is no building as yet, and it will be useless to
construct sheds on that dock to handle traffic until the breakwater in question is built. The government have already constructed the foundation but the wharf is so exposed to the weather that until the Negro Point breakwater is built it will be very little used as a freight handling proposition. I do hope the government will bring down a supplementary estimate to take care of the Negro Point breakwater.
Now as to the point I spoke of first: Our farmers this year have been getting only a dollar a barrel for potatoes that cost them $2.50 a barrel. We have been getting less than 50 per cent of the cost of growing, and still we have been paying wharfage on our shipments over the wharf and through the shed the government provided for us this year and which we appreciate, I can assure the minister. Still I would like to insist that if this kind of traffic is not charged for over other government wharves, we should be refunded the money that we have paid this year and be relieved of the charge in the future.

I think my hon. friend is probably under a misconception. In the larger ports undoubtedly there must be wharfage charges made. It is in the small outlying communities w'here the individual brings his package to the wharf, or takes it from the wharf, where fees are probably not collected. In the case of the larger ports charges must be made for the freight or traffic going over the wharves.

I realize that it is
the practice but I am still not convinced of the justice of it. It is the same class of freight absolutely, and I doubt if there is very much freight handled out of Canada to-day that is paying the producer as little as potatoes are paying the New Brunswick farmer. As I said before we have not received over a dollar a barrel of 165 pounds for our crop of potatoes this year and it cost us $2.50 to grow them. Still we are paying wharfage fees when farmers who happen to live at smaller points of shipment apparently are not paying these fees.

I think the practice outlined by the minister is all right. The two cases are not analogous at all. The one case is the case of a small farmer bringing down his little cart load of stuff to send to the market, and the other case is that of a great export trade which runs into hundreds and thousands of dollars. As a matter of fact you never could collect wharfage on these little shipments, and nobody would ever be foolish enough to try it.
Supply-Public Works
It is a matter of principle.
In the case of the particular item under discussion, what is the nature of the traffic over this wharf? .

There are about
5,500	inhabitants. The exports are largely farm products; there having been exported last year 75,000 bushels of potatoes and 20,000 bushels of other vegetables; 80,000 pounds of butter; 800 head of cattle; $100,000 worth of pork, and 80,000 baskets of fruit.

I believe there are thirty-five of these wharves items in which money is expended to repair wharves. In some cases it is mentioned as "wharves repaired"-just a little variety. How many of these have had to pay any interest at all? I was thinking it was rather strange that so much money was being expended without any thought that the people using those facilities should pay the interest thereon, as has been pointed out by the right hon. leader of the Opposition. In the case of grain elevators and similar facilities we expect to pay a rate that will enable them to pay their way. An hon. member on the other side was referring to the fact that he had asked the government on several occasions to have these improvements made, and now that he had succeeded in his request I could not help thinking of the times that the farmers in certain districts-not one but many-have asked for branch lines that were already graded to be completed. In many cases the ties and rails were lying there ready to be laid down, and yet they ' have been refused. Surely it is not good business. However, I will not discuss that matter now, but I hope the same generosity as is shown by the government at this time, in going forward with new work because it seems to be needed, will be exhibited when the Minister of Railways brings down his estimates and we take up the discussion of branch lines.
Do the railways ,out west pay any more interest on the capital invested than the railways in these other provinces?
The western railways pay all right, but it is the hon. member's "idols of the past" built in between that do not pay.
I assure hon. members that the railways in the West are the railways above all others in the Dominion that help to make the dividends.
Is that the case of the Hudson Bay?
Yes, there has been a grant set aside for the building of that line for many years back.

I can give my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) a case in which one of these wharves has brought some revenue to the country. We have a small wharf in my own constituency that cost the government $22,000. It was built 21 years ago, and since that time it has afforded free wharfage to 1,500 fishermen. It has been the means of bringing to the railways of this country an average of 365 carloads of freight every year. This shows what a small wharf built in a fishing section can bring to this country in the way of revenue. I believe that, so far as wharf accommodation is concerned, it should be left free to the fishermen. I think the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has overlooked the fact that for the past 50 years, in fact since confederation, the fishermen of this country have enjoyed free wharfage on all the wharves built in the Dominion of Canada, and I believe that money spent for the building of wharves at the gateway of the country is money spent, to the advantage, not only to the fishermen of eastern Canada, but of the agriculturists of western Canada and all the provilnces of this Dominion.

I am not rising to criticize the estimates at the present time, but to make a suggestion, which suggestion was made and acted upon in this House two years ago, when the little group I belonged to occupied a small pen down in the corner, where they could not hear anything when the estimates were going through.
The hon. member calls it a pen.

At that time we asked that the minister when putting through his estimates might move down nearer the middle of the chamber. The "not still small voice" at all, but the voice of New Brunswick reminded me that some hon. members down in that end of the chamber do not hear a word of what is going on up here, and I would ask the Minister of Public Works, and the other ministers who still have their estimates to put through, if they would adopt that suggestion. We in this section of the House are entitled to hear everything that is going on, but a great many hon. members do not hear anything at all.

I do not like to appear in the role of a pedagogue towards the government party; but I really think it would contribute to the usefulness of this Chamber if the government would see to it that some little preliminary instruction was given to its members on the facts associated with the government's estimates. There has never been a dollar of public money spent towards any amusement ground in Toronto, and I do not think there is in this Dominion a city that has itself contributed so much towards those purposes for which, in other places, the Dominion government provides, as has the city of Toronto. ^ If the hon. member will commence his oration by showing that a dollar has gone to any amusement purpose in Toronto out of the treasury of Canada, from that on there will be an intelligible lesson to be drawn from his remarks. But the onus is on him to show that, and it cannot be done. Not only can he not show that; but he cannot succeed in showing that the city of T oronto itself has not done very much that, in other places, has been wholly done by the Dominion government in the way of navigation and port facilities.
I withdraw absolutely nothing of the remarks which I have just made, notwithstanding what the leader of the Opposition has said. As to the lesson which he has intended to give me-
I meant that his minister should give it.

-I might say to the right hon. gentleman that I know parliamentary rules and customs well enough to dispense with any lesson from him. I have shown this on former occasions, and if my right hon.

friend again uses towards another hon. member in this House the fatherly language which he has just adopted, he may find that I am a rather unruly child.

That the hon. member is an unruly child, I have found out already; I do not need that lesson again. I did not suggest that he did not know the rules of the House. I know he does. I suggest that before he endeavours to raise some fun at the expense of Toronto by intimating that it has received special favours, he owes it to this House to prove that the money of Canada has gone to afford amusements for the people of Toronto. That he has not done, and that he cannot do.

It is a pity hon. members are not better posted when they get up to speak. I would tell my hon. friend across the way that this is not to add to the harbour, but to protect the eastern entrance to the bay, which is government property and the city gets no benefit from it whatever.
Is not the bay in the harbour?
No, sir.
Or the harbour in the bay?
The harbour is on this side of the bay. If my hon. friend will come to Toronto-
I am going next week.

-and see what sports we
have there, he will be very well satisfied.

Before the item carries I wish to state the position in which the hon. member for Dorchester places himself by declining to withdraw a remark which we are told upon authority is untrue, namely, that of asserting something which he cannot prove.
